CITATION
:

Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa v. S.K
. 2015 ONSC 4623

OTTAWA
COURT FILE NO.:
13-2997

DATE:
2015/07/17

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

HEARD:
May 27, 2015
(Ottawa)

REASONS
FOR Judgment

Parfett J.

[
1
]

The Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa (“CAS”)
requests a summary judgment with respect to this protection application, dated
December 23, 2013, relating to the child K.K. (D.O.B. XX XX, 2011).  In their
initial pleadings, the Society requested an order placing the child in the care
of the mother, S.K., subject to the supervision of the CAS.  Since the time of
the original application the Society has concluded that if the child is with
her mother and there is no access with the father, P.K., there are no
protection concerns.  Consequently, the CAS requests a finding that K.K. is a
child in need of protection with respect to the father and an order placing the
child in the sole custody of her mother, with no access to the father, pursuant
to
s. 57.1
of the
Child and Family Services Act
[1]
(“
CFSA
”).

[
2
]

The mother consents to the finding that K.K. is
a child in need of protection and to the order of sole custody.  In addition,
the mother requests:

•

That guideline child support be paid by P.K.;

•

Permission to move out of the province without
providing her address to P.K.; and,

•

A restraining order prohibiting P.K. from having
any contact, directly or indirectly, with S.K. or K.K.

[
3
]

The father opposes the requested orders and
requests that the CAS withdraw their application. He wishes to resolve matters
with S.K. without court involvement.

[
4
]

For the reasons that follow, the Court grants
the summary judgment motion and makes the following orders:

1.

K.K. is a child in need of protection pursuant to s. 37(2)(b), risk
of physical harm, and s. 37(2)(g), risk of emotional harm, of the
CFSA
;

2.

K.K.’s birth, parentage and religion is found in accordance with the
mother’s affidavit at volume 1, tab 7 of the continuing record;

3.

Sole custody is granted to the mother pursuant to
s. 57.1
of the
CFSA
;

4.

The father will have no access to K.K.;

5.

A restraining order is granted prohibiting P.K. from direct or
indirect contact with either S.K. or K.K. and from being within 500 meters of
their places of residence, employment or education or within 100 meters of any
other place where they may attend; and,

6.

S.K. is granted permission to move both herself and K.K. out of the province
without providing an address to P.K.

[
5
]

The issue of child support will have to be dealt with at a later date as
there was no financial evidence provided by either party.

Procedural issues

[
6
]

At the outset of the summary judgment motion, counsel for the CAS raised
concerns that P.K. appeared in his affidavit to be requesting an adjournment to
obtain counsel in order to respond to the report of Dr. Sutton.

[
7
]

The Court asked P.K. how he wished to proceed. He indicated that,
contrary to the statements made in his affidavit, he did not want to adjourn
the motion.  It was pointed out to P.K. that he had options available to him to
possibly retain counsel. It was also made clear that the Court would be willing
to grant P.K. an adjournment to obtain counsel and to permit him to have Dr.
Sutton’s report reviewed and critiqued by another psychiatrist.  P.K. was
adamant that he did not want to adjourn the motion, and so the matter
proceeded.

Background

Chronology of events prior to protection application

[
8
]

The parents began their relationship in 1997.
According to both parties, it was a dysfunctional relationship from the start.
The parties separated and reunited several times over the course of the relationship.
[2]

[
9
]

In March 2000, P.K. assaulted S.K.  He was
charged with assault and ultimately pleaded guilty to the charge.  He received
a sentence of 30 days jail.
[3]

The parties continued their relationship and married on August 24, 2008.  They
separated in January 2009, but reunited once again in September 2009.  S.K.
became pregnant in the summer of 2010, and K.K. was born in […] 2011.
[4]
The parties had
separated in September 2010, but S.K. returned to live with P.K. after the
birth of their child.  The final separation occurred in July 2011.

[
10
]

Between July 2011 and March 2013, P.K. exercised
access to K.K.  According to S.K., P.K.’s access visits were sometimes
supervised by her, while other times P.K. had the child alone.  According to
S.K., the access could go well or be difficult.
[5]

[
11
]

In early January 2013, S.K. informed P.K. that
she wanted to visit her sister in Alberta for two months and that she intended
to take K.K. with her.  P.K. objected to this proposal.  On January 11, 2013,
P.K. sent a series of text messages to S.K. stating:

1.

“You will pay for any attempt to take [K.K.]
from the province for a long period without my consent. Not a threat, just a
warning.”

2.

“Your final warning!  I will take severe
irreversible action from now on.  No more words just payback for wrongdoings
stupid c**t.”

3.

“I’m sick of you pieces of shit attacking me,
attempting to murder me and then cowardly lying to make me out to be the bad
guy…May death come to all of you!”
[6]

[
12
]

In March 2013, P.K. continued to send abusive
text messages to S.K., including one that stated:

I promise ur not
taking [K.K.] across Canada and no amount of police help will be enough.  I’m
ready for war bitch!  Whatever is gonna happen it will be on you and ur
families head. Don’t you dare think of putting K in the battlefield as a human
shield dumbass.  You know what happens on the battlefield!! You’ve been warned!
[7]

[
13
]

On March 30, 2013, the Ottawa Police Service
(OPS) was called to P.K.’s residence regarding an allegation of assault that
had apparently occurred on March 27, 2013.  According to S.K., P.K. grabbed her
by the back of the head and spit on her during a re-enactment of a fight that
P.K. had with S.K.’s brothers.  When she tried to leave, P.K. allegedly pulled
her hair.  Ultimately, he let her leave and S.K. called the police.
[8]
The OPS called
the CAS as there was a child present during this dispute.  The CAS began an
investigation.

[
14
]

On April 10, 2013, the partner assault
investigator called P.K. to tell him he would be charged.  Subsequently, P.K.
sent a number of text messages to S.K. begging her to reconsider.
[9]
S.K. recanted her
allegation of assault.
[10]

Consequently, no charges were laid in respect of this incident.

[
15
]

After investigating the allegation of domestic
violence, the CAS recommended that access be negotiated and potentially
supervised.  P.K. was not happy with this recommendation and consequently,
access did not occur.  P.K. was upset about his lack of access and he began to sending
threatening text messages to S.K. demanding access.
[11]
In addition, he
began calling the CAS worker, Melanie Guibord, leaving her multiple voicemail
messages.
[12]

[
16
]

On April 26, 2013, the CAS advised P.K. that it
was their position that his access to K.K. should be supervised.  P.K. objected
to the supervised access. Nonetheless, a visit was organized prior to S.K.
leaving for her visit to Alberta in May of 2013.
[13]

[
17
]

On July 13, 2013, P.K sent the following message
to S.K.:

If I can’t be a
dad to my baby then you will not be a mom to her either!!!  You will get tenfold
what you give and go ahead and call the pigs and show them these texts.
Whatever mistakes you make will be neutralized indefinitely…I don’t give a fuck
if doing the right thing cost me my life c**t!  Anyone who fucks with me better
be prepared for the consequences, even the pigs bitch! You know I’m what I’m
capable of c**t! I will legally make all you pieces of shit pay the ultimate
price…
[14]

[
18
]

On July 31, 2013, while S.K. was still in
Alberta, P.K. sent the following text message to her: “I would sooner slice ur
throat than have another supervised visit! Capish!”  Consequently, on August 1,
2013, S.K. filed a motion without notice, seeking interim sole custody of K.K.,
no access to P.K. and a restraining order against P.K.  The order was granted.
After notice was given to P.K., the matter was heard again on September 13,
2013, and the interim order was continued.  In his endorsement, the judge noted:
“I am not confident that the Mr. [P.K.] is not a threat to the child at this
time.”

[
19
]

On August 2, 2013, the CAS informed P.K. that
they were now recommending no access between him and his daughter.
[15]

[
20
]

In November 2013, S.K. visited P.K.’s parents’
home on several occasions and permitted access between P.K. and K.K, despite
the fact that there was a restraining order in place and the CAS recommended no
access.  According to S.K., she was manipulated into permitting access and although
there were no significant problems with the visits, she was very uncomfortable
with the situation.
[16]

[
21
]

On December 4, 2013, the court ordered
supervised access between P.K. and K.K.  The Society attempted to approve
supervisors, but the only proposed supervisor they were permitted to contact
was P.K.’s father; and the Society would not approve him.
[17]

[
22
]

The CAS continued to be concerned in relation to
the child given P.K.’s history of unstable and sometimes violent behaviour and
S.K.’s reluctance to follow the CAS’s recommendations regarding access.  On
December 23, 2013, the CAS filed the current application.

Police contacts with P.K
.

[
23
]

Apart from the assault conviction in 2000, there
have been numerous contacts between P.K. and the police.

[
24
]

On January 6, 2002, P.K. was arrested for
robbery, theft and extortion.
[18]

[
25
]

On March 12, 2002, P.K was charged with failure
to comply with his undertaking as a consequence of contacting a complainant.
[19]

[
26
]

On April 1, 2002 P.K. was arrested for issuing a
death threat to a police officer and causing a disturbance arising out of an
incident at the police station.
[20]

[
27
]

On April 13, 2004, police were called to
investigate an allegation that P.K. was leaving aggressive and intimidating
voicemail messages for an insurance adjuster.
[21]

[
28
]

On July 15, 2004, P.K.’s probation officer
reported to police that he had received threats from P.K.
[22]

[
29
]

On May 23, 2005 an officer who had charged P.K.
with uttering threats received six voicemail messages from P.K.  The messages
contained profanity and implied violence.
[23]

[
30
]

On February 1, 2008, police received a call from
P.K.  He was irate concerning recent dealings with the police and indicated
that he was having visions of decapitation and torture of the female police
officer and her children.  He stated that he and the power to kill with his
bare hands and was a trained fighter.
[24]

[
31
]

On June 27, 2009, P.K. reported receiving
harassing phone calls from his ex-wife.
[25]

P.K. did not want to lay charges and did not want the police to contact S.K.
The file was closed without further action.
[26]

[
32
]

December 10, 2010, police received a call from a
Canadian Tire store.  P.K. told police he had been assaulted by his former
brothers-in-law.  Police determined that the fight was mutual and refused to
lay charges.  P.K. was upset by the decision and told the investigating police
officer that he could stab his wife in the stomach.  He also indicated that he
would not file a complaint but would retaliate.
[27]

[
33
]

On September 29, 2011, an employee of Service
Ontario complained to police that P.K. threatened “you’re gonna be sorry that
you did not help me when you’re finished work.”  At the end of the work day,
P.K. was standing near the employee’s car.  P.K. bragged to the employee about
his large police file.
[28]

[
34
]

August 12, 2012, P.K. went to a drive through at
a McDonald’s restaurant and tried to order food.  The system was down and P.K.
was advised that no food could be obtained.  He proceeded to be rude and
aggressive to the McDonald’s workers.  They called the police.  The police
arrived and noted that P.K. appeared to have been drinking.  He was asked to
provide a sample of his breath into a roadside screening device and he
refused.  Consequently, P.K. was charged criminally.  P.K. proceeded to harass
the two officers involved in the case by leaving lengthy and aggressive
voicemail messages.  He repeatedly called the officers ‘terrorists’.  He
indicated in one message that he was very powerful, both intellectually and
physically.  In another message he suggested that he would like to fight one of
the officers.  He also told the police that he would not comply with any of the
police demands and would “fight this to the death.”
[29]

[
35
]

In 2014, P.K. was found guilty of some of the
criminal charges related to the 2012 incident.
[30]

[
36
]

In addition to leaving voicemail messages with
the police, P.K. also called the McDonald’s restaurant head office and threatened
their customer service representatives.  As a consequence of this behaviour,
P.K. was again arrested and charged with threats and harassment.

[
37
]

P.K. filed a civil suit against both the OPS and
McDonald’s restaurant.  That civil suit is ongoing.
[31]

[
38
]

On February 20, 2013, a police officer filed a
complaint as a result of P.K. leaving him a voicemail message, in which he
threatened to: “beat the living shit out [the officer’s] skull.”

[
39
]

On November 13, 2013, there was an altercation
at a construction site. P.K. was signalled to stop by a worker but chose not to;
he drove through and ‘nudged’ the worker with his car.  The worker got upset
and banged on the hood of P.K.’s car.  P.K. got out of his car, threatened to
kill the worker, got back into his car and then sped off.  The police were
called to the scene, but P.K. was gone.  The decision was made to issue P.K.
with a police warning instead of charging him criminally.  P.K. subsequently called
the police station looking for the investigating officer, but ended up speaking
with a police dispatcher. He was noted as being rude, demeaning and
aggressive.  He also left threatening messages for the investigating officer.
[32]

Events after Protection Application was filed

[
40
]

In January 2014, shortly after the Protection Application
was filed, P.K. began leaving numerous voicemail messages for the CAS caseworker.
The messages were rambling and very aggressive in tone.
[33]

[
41
]

In the messages, P.K. alleged that S.K. lied to
the Society.  He also accused the Society of pressuring S.K. into maintaining
her lies with the threat of taking the child away from her.  He suggested that,
contrary to the allegation of domestic violence made by S.K., S.K. was in fact
the aggressive one, which was why he divorced her.

[
42
]

P.K. called the caseworker a ‘terrorist’,
accused her of abusing her authority, threatened a civil suit for defamation if
the Society did not ‘back off’, and accused the Society of ‘torturing’ his
daughter by denying him access.  He suggested that the case worker “otta do
swan dives off a cliff for humanity’s sake” and went on to suggest that in a
different era, the case worker would be “burned at the stake like all evil
witches, dark witches.”
[34]

[
43
]

A portion of one message reads as follows:

I’m never going to comply
with terrorists you guys have been you have been deemed a criminal ok you have
you have already been convicted in God’s court of law that you’re a criminal,
you assaulted and abused my daughter directly or indirectly ok and you’re
assaulting and abusing your position of authority assaulting and abusing me and
maliciously prosecuting me ok you’re you’re everything that I have said you
have been found guilty of in the court of God’s law now you’re going to be
found guilty of it in Ontario in the court of Ontario law and I will never
comply with terrorists I will never comply with any one of your requests not
one of them.
[35]

[
44
]

In a later message, P.K. indicates that he wants
“all terrorists to be tortured to death.”
[36]

[
45
]

As a consequence of these messages, P.K. was
arrested and charged with a number of criminal offences. He was initially
detained in custody, and then released on strict bail conditions. He was not to
contact the CAS, except through counsel and only in writing.  On the day of
this motion, P.K. advised the Court that he plead guilty to one count of
threats in relation to this incident.

Mental health assessment

[
46
]

Subsequent to filing the protection application,
the CAS requested disclosure of any police reports in relation to P.K.  After
receiving the reports and given P.K.’s behaviour towards the caseworker, the
Society had concerns regarding P.K.’s mental health.

[
47
]

At the first appearance on January 2, 2014, the CAS
requested a mental health assessment of P.K.  A motion was heard on May 13,
2014. The Court granted the order for a mental health assessment, pursuant to

s. 54
of the
CFSA
.  P.K. was given the option of completing the
assessment with the Society’s choice of psychiatrist or a psychiatrist of his
own choosing.  P.K. chose Dr. Helen Ward, who is a forensic psychiatrist with
the Royal Ottawa Hospital.

[
48
]

The CAS sought confirmation that Dr. Ward
understood the terms of reference of the s. 54 assessment and asked P.K.
to have Dr. Ward contact them.  His response was a lengthy email in which he stated
in part:

I will never comply with
you criminals even if it means I will never see [K.K.] again!  It’s Dr. Ward or
nothing!  She is doing the assessment and you criminal terrorists should back
off!  I never wanted for any of this to happen but yall are leaving me no
choice but to express my frustrations with the pain and suffering yall have caused
on my daughter and I in a completely criminal and terrorist fashion.
[37]

[
49
]

In an email sent a short time later, P.K. lauded
his own restraint and indicated that “having many people – officers of the
court – tell lies about me to judges and judges allowing themselves to be
fooled/biased by these obvious lies!  This would be enough to make anyone of
you go crazy and pull a Moncton move but not me!”
[38]

[
50
]

On December 4, 2014, Dr. Ward issued her
report.  In her opening paragraph, Dr. Ward confirmed that she had a copy of
the Court’s endorsement, and that she understood she was doing an assessment
pursuant to
s. 54
of the
CFSA
.
[39]

[
51
]

Dr. Ward indicated that she met with P.K. on
nine occasions.  She also reviewed: a number of documents from the family law
application, a transcript of voicemail messages left by P.K. for the case
worker, the OPS charging sheet in relation to the voicemail messages left for
the case worker, as well as a large volume of documents from the child
protection file.

[
52
]

She notes that P.K.’s thought form was:

[N]otable for being
over-inclusive and often circumstantial (going through a great deal of material
before coming back to the point).  He often appeared overconfident and he
expressed great faith in his abilities to overcome obstacles.  He also appeared
to overstate his previous accomplishments although he appeared to genuinely
believe his own statements about them.  A notable theme for [P.K.] was his
opinion that certain members of the Ottawa police as well as certain court
officials and CAS, had lied or misrepresented things in order to put him in a
bad light.  While he occasionally used terms such as conspiracy, it was evident
…that he does not actually have a delusional belief that there is a conspiracy
against him.  Rather, he holds a strong belief in the moral correctness of his
own argument and a belief that he has been ‘bullied’ and needs to persevere in
order to receive ‘fair treatment’.
[40]

[
53
]

Dr. Ward indicated that her ‘diagnostic
impression’ was that P.K. did not have a psychotic or major mood disorder.
Instead, in her view, P.K. met the diagnostic criteria for obsessive compulsive
personality disorder and narcissistic personality disorder.
[41]

[
54
]

In her conclusion, Dr. Ward stated that P.K.’s
risk of physical harm to others is low, but the risk of P.K. continuing to
treat others in an aggressive and inappropriate manner is high. Dr. Ward agreed
with S.K.’s assertion that shared custody between S.K. and P.K would be
impossible.
[42]

In conclusion, Dr. Ward stated:

[I]t is my
psychiatric opinion that [P.K.] could safely manage supervised access with [K.K.]
and that he could progress to unsupervised access with support and time.   The
big problem would be in finding a supervising person or agency that he would be
able to deal with properly, and in figuring out a progression towards
unsupervised access.

[
55
]

Dr. Peter Sutton conducted a file review for the
CAS.  His review was very thorough and included a review of Dr. Ward’s report.
He agreed with Dr. Ward’s conclusion that P.K. met the criteria for both obsessive
compulsive disorder and narcissistic personality disorder, but added that he
believed that P.K. also met the criteria for paranoid personality disorder.
[43]

[
56
]

Dr. Sutton took issue with Dr. Ward’s conclusion
that P.K had shown “relatively scant problematic behaviour towards his daughter”
and that he could probably modify his behaviour around his daughter with
relative ease.  According to Dr. Sutton, before making such a determination,
Dr. Ward ought to have sought out information from other people such as S.K.,
the CAS and other collateral informants.  He also noted that Dr. Ward’s
conclusion “does not appear to take into consideration [P.K.’s] very long
history of enraged opposition to authority, and the fact that any access plan
would deprive him of the control which he appears to feel is his due.”
[44]

[
57
]

Furthermore, Dr. Sutton expressed concern that
Dr. Ward had not addressed the risk of possible psychological harm to K.K. if
P.K. exercised his access.  He noted that “the exposure to adult conflict of
various kinds can be damaging to a child, particularly in a situation as
problematic as the present one in which there is very little evidence of
reflectiveness in the parent or the inter-parental system, and it needs to be
taken seriously.”
[45]

[
58
]

Dr. Sutton expressed dismay at Dr. Ward’s
conclusion that it would be safe for P.K. to have supervised access moving
towards unsupervised access with his daughter.  He stated:

Unless there are
exceptional circumstances it is inappropriate to make recommendations about
custody and access without having interviewed both parents and any other
caregivers, important collaterals and the child and/or observed the child with
the parents.  In this case, it would not have been possible for Dr. Ward to
have observed [K.K.] with [P.K.].  The importance of these parts of an
assessment are clearly laid out in numerous sets of guidelines concerning
custody and access.
[46]

[
59
]

Finally, Dr. Sutton disagreed with Dr. Ward’s
finding that it was unfair to judge P.K.’s future behaviour based on his
behaviour during the course of the child protection and family law
proceedings.  He observed that P.K. “has repeatedly reacted in a problematic
manner” and that the “record going back to 1999 suggest[s] that [P.K.] [has]
chronic difficulty in managing frustration and interpersonal negotiation, and
furthermore, repeatedly [gets] himself into trouble because of [his] character
traits”
[47]

consisting of automatic suspiciousness, oppositionality, and a lurking sense
that authorities are out to harm him.
[48]

[
60
]

In his own conclusion, Dr. Sutton pointed out that
what he did was a file review, not a clinical assessment; therefore, there were
significant limitations in terms of what conclusions he could properly draw.
[49]

Issues

[
61
]

On a motion for summary judgment, the key issue
to be decided is whether there is a genuine issue for trial based on the
evidence before the court. If there is, the issue becomes whether a trial can
be avoided using the new powers under Rules 20.04(2.1) and (2.2), provided the
use of those powers is not against the interests of justice.
[50]

[
62
]

The issues to be considered are:

1.

Whether K.K. is a child in need of protection?

2.

Whether a custody order pursuant to
s. 57.1
of the
CFSA
is in
K.K.’s best interests?

3.

What, if any, access to P.K. is in K.K.’s best interests?

Positions of the parties

[
63
]

The CAS is concerned about P.K.’s mental health
as well as his aggressiveness towards S.K. and others in the community.  In
particular, the Society is concerned that, if P.K. is allowed access with his
daughter he may become fixated on ensuring that his daughter understands the
alleged injustices perpetrated against him by S.K., her family, the OPS, the CAS,
the Crown Attorney’s office and the courts.  In addition, the Society is
concerned that P.K. will expose his daughter to aggression and violence against
others. P.K.’s unwillingness to follow any service provider’s directions with
respect to his supervised access is also problematic.

[
64
]

S.K. echoes the Society’s concerns and contends
that, due to P.K.’s long term harassment and harmful behaviours towards her,
his uncontrollable and inappropriate behaviour towards others in the community,
and his lack of insight into his own behaviour, P.K. would threaten the
emotional stability of K.K. Consequently, it is not in K.K.’s best interests to
have access with her father.

[
65
]

P.K. asks that the Society withdraw the
Protection Application and allow him and S.K. to pursue an amicable solution together,
solely based on K.K.’s best interests.  He seeks immediate supervised access to
K.K.  In addition, P.K. asks that if the application is not withdrawn then it
should proceed to trial.  He argues that the size of this file and the numerous
issues in dispute mandate a trial.

Summary Judgment Motion

Legislative Framework

[
66
]

Under Rule 16(1) of the
Family Law Rules
[51]

(“
FLR
”), a party may bring a motion for summary judgment for a final
order without a trial on all or part of a claim. This includes cases under the
CFSA

(
Rule 16(2)
). If there is no genuine issue requiring trial, the court must grant
summary judgment (Rule 16(6)). If the only genuine issue is a question of law,
the court must decide the issue and make a final order (Rules 16(7) and (8)).

[
67
]

In terms of evidence, the moving party must
serve an affidavit or other evidence that sets out the specific facts showing
that there is no genuine issue requiring trial (Rule 16(4)). The responding
party may not rest on mere allegations or denials, but must set out, in an
affidavit or other evidence, specific facts showing that there is a genuine
issue for trial (Rule 16(4.1)).

[
68
]

Rule 16(6.1) permits a judge to weigh evidence,
evaluate credibility and draw factual inferences, unless it is in the interests
of justice for these powers to only be exercised at trial.

[
69
]

If the court does not grant summary judgment, or
only grants it in part, the court may: (a) specify what facts are not in
dispute, state the issues and give directions about how and when the case will
go to trial (in which case the order governs how the trial proceeds, unless the
trial judge orders otherwise to prevent injustice); (b) give directions; and
(c) impose conditions (Rule 16(9)).

General Principles

[
70
]

Hryniak v. Mauldin
[52]

dealt with a summary judgment motion under Rule 20 of the
Rules of Civil
Procedure
(the “
RCP
”).
[53]

Justice Karakatsanis, writing for a unanimous court, called for balance as well
as recognition “that a process can be fair and just, without the expense and
delay of a trial, and that alternative models of adjudication are no less
legitimate than the conventional trial.”
[54]

According to the Court, achieving balance in the justice system:

…requires a shift in
culture. The principal goal remains the same: a fair process that results in a
just adjudication of disputes. A fair and just process must permit a judge to
find the facts necessary to resolve the dispute and to apply the relevant legal
principles to the facts as found. However, that process is illusory unless it
is also accessible — proportionate, timely and affordable. The proportionality
principle means that the best forum for resolving a dispute is not always that
with the most painstaking procedure.
[55]

[
71
]

In keeping with these principles, the test for
when summary judgment should be granted is as follows:

There will be no genuine
issue requiring trial when the judge is able to reach a fair and just
determination on the merits on a motion for summary judgment. This will be the
case when the process (1) allows the judge to make the necessary findings of
fact, (2) allows the judge to apply the law to the facts, and (3) is a
proportionate, more expeditious and less expensive means to achieve a just
result.
[56]

Hryniak
also sets out the following key principles with respect to summary
judgment:

•

The overarching issue to be answered is “whether
summary judgment will provide a fair and just adjudication.”
[57]
In deciding
whether summary judgment will be fair, it is important to note that “the
standard for fairness is not whether the procedure is as exhaustive as a trial,
but whether it gives the judge confidence that she can find the necessary facts
and apply the relevant legal principles so as to resolve the dispute.”
[58]

•

The new fact-finding powers under Rule
20.04(2.1)—which allow motion judges to weigh evidence, evaluate credibility
and draw inferences—are presumptively available; judges are allowed to exercise
them unless it is in the interests of justice that they only be exercised at
trial.
[59]

•

Where a matter is to proceed to trial, the
motion judge should also seize herself of the matter as the trial judge, and
courts should be prepared to change their scheduling practices in order to
facilitate this outcome.
[60]

[
72
]

Justice Karakatsanis set out a roadmap for
motion judges in summary judgment proceedings:

On a motion for summary
judgment under Rule 20.04, the judge should first determine if there is a
genuine issue requiring trial based only on the evidence before her, without
using the new fact-finding powers.  There will be no genuine issue requiring a
trial if the summary judgment process provides her with the evidence required
to fairly and justly adjudicate the dispute and is a timely, affordable and
proportionate procedure, under Rule 20.04(2)(a).  If there appears to be a
genuine issue requiring a trial, she should then determine if the need for a
trial can be avoided by using the new powers under Rules 20.04(2.1) and (2.2).
She may, at her discretion, use those powers, provided that their use is not
against the interest of justice.  Their use will not be against the interest of
justice if they will lead to a fair and just result and will serve the goals of
timeliness, affordability and proportionality in light of the litigation as a
whole.
[61]

[

While

]

principles underlying its interpretation are of

]

phase of Rule 20 are also relevant to the post-motion phase under Rule 16. In

[66]

]

Similarly, in

The Supreme Court

Procedure

(Ontario)

principles.

disposition of issues in appropriate circumstances as much as any other area of

[emphasis added]

While “the use, scope and evidentiary basis for

Summary judgment in child protection matters

[
80
]

With respect to child protection cases, the courts
have long held that Rule 16 applies.  However, the case law indicates that, in
granting summary judgment, the court must exercise caution in keeping with the
principles of justice, fairness and the best interests of the child.

[71]

[
81
]

With respect to the need to proceed cautiously,
courts have held as follows:

•

A court seized of a motion for summary judgment
in a child protection case must “take a good hard look at the merits” to
determine if there is a genuine issue for trial.
[72]

•

While caution is important, it is nevertheless
the case that “[i]f the evidence does not raise a triable issue as to where the
best interests lie, those best interests themselves call for a resolution
without the delay associated with the trial and the resulting prolongation of
the state of uncertainty about the child’s future.”
[73]

•

Extra caution is needed in cases where the
resisting party is unrepresented.
[74]

•

Motion judges “should be very cautious in
granting summary judgment in child protection cases, since the stakes for the
family are so high and the granting of summary judgment deprives the parent of
his day in court and the procedural safeguard of cross-examination of witnesses
before a judge.”
[75]

[
82
]

Other principles that courts have developed to
determine the appropriateness of summary judgment include the following:

•

“A triable issue is one which is relevant to the
issues to be decided. The test is whether the question at issue is a foregone
conclusion. There may be a factual dispute on an issue, but that does not
necessarily raise a triable issue if the balance of the admitted and undisputed
evidence leads to an inevitable outcome. If, for example, it is a foregone
conclusion, based on the admitted and undisputed evidence, that the best
interests of the child require an order for Crown wardship, then there is no
genuine issue for trial. While there may be issues to be decided, the question
is whether they are issues that require trial.”
[76]

•

Parties must put their best foot forward; in
other words, they “must lead trump or risk losing.”
[77]

•

The moving party has the onus of establishing
there is no genuine issue requiring trial. Once the moving party establishes a
prima
facie
case, the onus shifts to the responding party to show that there is a
genuine issue requiring trial.
[78]
The determination of whether there is a genuine issue requiring
trial is specific to the circumstances of a particular case including the
nature of the order being made.
[79]

•

“While it may not be appropriate in the face of
the child’s best interests and the new rules to suggest that the parent’s
position must be ‘untenable’ in order to resort to summary proceedings, it is
clear that the nature of the evidence to be before the court, the
reasonableness of any potential plans and the statutory time frames all have a
role to play in the determination of whether there is a genuine issue for trial.”
[80]

•

The legal process is not to be used as a
strategy to “buy time” to develop an ability to parent. In child protection
proceedings, the genuineness of an issue must arise from something more than a
parent’s heartfelt expression of his desire to resume care of the child; the
parent’s evidence must support that he faces better prospects than what existed
at the time the society removed the child from his care and that he has
developed new parenting skills.
[81]

What impact do the new powers under Rule 16 have on the
process?

[

Amendments to Rule 16 came into force on May 2,
2015. These amendments, among other things, import the expanded fact-finding
powers from Rule 20 of the
RCP
to Rule 16 of the
FLR
. The relevant
provision provides as follows:

(6.1) In
determining whether there is a genuine issue requiring a trial, the court shall
consider the evidence submitted by the parties, and the court may exercise any
of the following powers for the purpose, unless it is in the interest of
justice for such powers to be exercised only at a trial:

1.

Weighing the evidence.

2.

Evaluating the credibility of a deponent.

3.

Drawing any reasonable inference from the
evidence.
[82]

[
84

The principles enunciated in

•

A court should first determine whether summary
judgment should be granted without using the enhanced powers under rule
20.04(2.1);

•

The new fact-finding powers are presumptively
available; judges are allowed to exercise them unless it is in the interests of
justice that they only be exercised at trial;

•

The inquiry into the interests of justice is
comparative. Proportionality is assessed in relation to the full trial, and involves
comparing the relative cost and speed of the two procedures, as well as the
availability of evidence and the opportunity to evaluate it;

•

Whether it is against the “interest of justice”
to use the new fact-finding powers will often coincide with whether there is a
“genuine issue requiring trial”; and,

•

The “interest of justice” inquiry also considers
the consequences of the motion in the context of the litigation as a whole.
[83]

Finding of Supervised access

[
128
]

The final issue to be addressed is P.K.’s
access.

[
129
]

At the outset, I want to state that it is clear
that P.K. loves his daughter very much and that he would not deliberately do
anything that he understood would harm her.

[
130
]

Unfortunately, the issue is whether P.K.
understands the extent to which his behaviour will inevitably harm his daughter,
even though he did not intend it to do so.  Alternatively, the issue is whether
P.K. can learn to modify his behaviour sufficiently and within sufficient time
to mitigate any possible harm.

[
131
]

The test at this stage of the proceeding is
whether K.K.’s best interests can only be met by an order of no access.
Termination of a child’s right to visit and have a relationship with a parent
is a remedy that should only be ordered as a last resort.  While it is optimal
for the best interests of the child to be balanced with the rights of the
parent, where there is a clash between these interests, the best interests of
the child will be the deciding factor.
[121]

[
132
]

Section 37(3)
of the
CFSA
outlines the
factors to consider in determining the best interests of the child.  The
factors relevant to this case are as follows:

•

The child’s physical, mental and emotional
needs, and the appropriate care to meet those needs;

•

The child’s physical, mental and emotional level
of development;

•

The importance for the child’s development of a
positive relationship with a parent;

•

The child’s relationship and emotional ties to a
parent;

•

The importance of continuity in this child’s
care and the possible effect on the child of disruption of that continuity;

•

The risk that the child may suffer harm through
being kept away from the care of a parent; and,

•

The degree of risk, if any, that justified the
finding that the child is in need of protection.

[
133
]

In the case of
Young v. Young
[122]
, the Supreme
Court of Canada considered the application of the best interests test in the
context of access.  Justice McLachlin noted:

I conclude that the
ultimate criterion for determining limits on access to a child is the best interests
of the child.  The custodial parent has no “right” to limit access.  The judge
must consider all factors relevant to determining what is in the child’s best
interests; a factor which must be considered in all cases is Parliament’s view
that contact with each parent is to be maximized to the extent that this is compatible
with the best interests of the child.  The risk of harm, to the child, while
not the ultimate legal test, may also be a factor to be considered.  This is
particularly so where the issue is the quality of access – what the access
parent [must] say or do with the child.  In such cases, it will generally be
relevant to consider whether the conduct in question poses a risk of harm to
the child which outweighs the benefits of a free and open relationship which
permits the child to know the access parent as he or she is.  It goes without
saying that, as for any other legal test, the judge, in determining what is in
the best interests of the child, must act not on his or her personal views, but
on the evidence.
[123]

[
134
]

The case law makes it clear that the benefit
referred to is the benefit to the child, not the parent.  The court must
determine whether, based on the evidence, the benefit to the child of
terminating access outweighs the benefit of continued contact.
[124]

[
135
]

Before terminating access, the court must
consider the alternative of supervised access.
[125]
In this case,
this is where the key issue lies.

[
136
]

]

]

]

]

•

•

[152]

•

[153]

•

In addition, Dr. Sutton observed that any
decision concerning whether it is in K.K.’s best interests to have access with

▪

The chronicity of [P.K.’s] psychological and

▪

Features of [P.K.’s] behaviour reflected in the

[P.K.’s] inability to submit himself

]

[
157
]

[
158
]

Taking into consideration all of the evidence, including
the evidence that there is

•

a risk of physical harm;

•

a risk of emotional harm;

•

that P.K. continues to lack insight into his
problematic behaviour;

•

the lack of evidence of any improvement brought
about through P.K.’s treatment;

•

the strong likelihood that no supervisor, acceptable
to P.K., could ever be found; and,

•

the evidence that P.K. continues to believe that

genuine issue for trial with respect to the issue of supervised access. The
evidence demonstrates clearly that the only order that would be in K.K.’s best
interests is an order terminating P.K.’s access.
